impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to a method of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments, reinstating a jury verdict of willful infringement by Eli Lilly. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent scope, particularly for genus claims covering antibody therapies where the specification discloses methods for making the claimed antibodies but only exemplifies one specific antibody.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug developers by affirming that disclosing known methods for producing a class of antibodies, combined with disclosure of a representative species, can satisfy written description and enablement requirements for broader genus claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar companies face greater difficulty challenging the validity of broad biologic patent claims, potentially extending market exclusivity periods for branded antibody therapies.

impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions using emulation and comparison to function call models are directed to abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101 at Alice step one, and whether foreign sales damages are recoverable for U.S. patent infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia against Norton (Gen Digital), finding the asserted cybersecurity patent claims abstract at Alice step one and requiring further proceedings at step two. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, limiting patent damages to domestic conduct. Enhanced damages and attorneys' fees were also set aside.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software and cybersecurity companies benefit from the reinforced limitation that patent damages cannot be based on foreign sales, and from continued robust application of the Alice framework to software-implemented inventions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting software-related patents face heightened § 101 eligibility risks, and university patent licensing programs may see reduced damages recoveries when infringers have substantial foreign revenue.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement and other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue for infringement and other substantive exclusionary rights has sufficient Article III standing even after granting an exclusive license. The court found the retained right to sue was not illusory given the licensor's control over enforcement and other retained rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses can retain enforcement rights and maintain standing to sue infringers, providing greater flexibility in patent licensing and monetization strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers will find it more difficult to challenge standing of patent owners who have licensed patents but retained litigation rights, reducing a potential defense avenue.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality grounds where accused processor designs were created domestically but manufactured and sold abroad, and whether VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory was properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit addressed extraterritoriality limits on patent infringement claims involving Intel's multicore processor technology, partially reversing the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement. The decision clarifies the geographic scope of U.S. patent rights in semiconductor and technology manufacturing contexts where design occurs domestically but production is offshore.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies with offshore manufacturing may benefit from clarification of extraterritoriality limits on U.S. patent infringement, particularly where design and manufacturing activities are split across jurisdictions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and patent holders may face challenges in capturing the full scope of infringement where accused products are designed in the U.S. but manufactured and sold abroad.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for tracking farming operations by collecting data from farming equipment, GPS, and implement profiles are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, finding the claims abstract, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, potentially opening the door to attorneys' fees for Farmers Edge. This decision reinforces the difficulty of patenting data collection and processing methods in the agricultural technology sector.
impacts.positiveImplications: Ag-tech companies accused of infringing data collection patents benefit from continued strict application of § 101 to claims that automate conventional data gathering and processing. The remand on exceptionality may enable fee recovery for defendants facing weak patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology innovators face significant barriers to obtaining and enforcing patents on precision farming data systems, and may face exceptional case findings if pursuing patents found ineligible under § 101.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet filed its trade secret misappropriation claim, where Insulet allegedly knew of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict in Insulet's favor on its DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow, holding that the statute of limitations had expired because Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. This decision significantly impacts how companies must act upon discovering potential trade secret theft by former employees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing a clear temporal defense against delayed claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face pressure to file misappropriation claims promptly upon discovering or having reason to know of potential theft, or risk losing their DTSA remedy entirely. Companies must implement robust monitoring and rapid legal response protocols.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that were generally known could constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship correction purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed patent inventorship correction, holding that generally known ideas cannot constitute an inventive contribution. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses benefit from the reinforced requirement that trade secret claimants must prove information derives independent economic value from not being generally known, raising the evidentiary bar for trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs and manufacturing processes face heightened risk of having claims rejected if the underlying concepts are found to be generally known in the industry.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify at summary judgment about matters outside personal knowledge to establish the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating engine controller reprogramming patents under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) deposition testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge and that computer source code commands are not hearsay statements. This decision has significant implications for patent invalidity defenses based on prior commercial activity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded ability to use corporate representative testimony and source code evidence to prove on-sale bar invalidity, even when original employees are unavailable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges as courts accept broader categories of evidence, including 30(b)(6) testimony from witnesses without firsthand knowledge of prior sales.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in denying JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility for communication technology patents, vacating eligibility for certain claims while affirming others, and affirming infringement and damages findings. The court's differentiated treatment of related claims based on their specific technical contributions provides important guidance on the Alice framework's application to telecommunications patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Standard-essential patent holders and communication technology companies benefit from the court's affirmance that some claims implementing specific technical improvements to constellation design are patent-eligible, preserving patent protection for innovations in digital communications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry communication standards face continued uncertainty as the court's claim-by-claim eligibility analysis may require costly and unpredictable litigation to determine which specific patent claims survive § 101 scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a single jury question covering infringement of multiple patents constitutes reversible error requiring a new trial, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 analysis under Alice step two for building automation system patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment and ordered a new trial, holding that a verdict form using a single infringement question for all asserted patents was reversible error because the jury could not identify which patent(s) were infringed. The court also remanded for further proceedings on § 101 eligibility for one patent while affirming eligibility for others.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must separately identify infringement of each asserted patent, preventing ambiguous verdicts that bundle multiple patents together.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement cases face additional procedural requirements for verdict forms and risk vacatur of favorable verdicts if the jury is not required to make patent-specific infringement findings.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed non-infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, holding that pH claim limitations refer to measurements at standard temperature conditions recognized in the pharmaceutical field. The court also affirmed that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents. This ruling impacts pharmaceutical patent claim drafting for formulation patents with temperature-dependent chemical parameters.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from the clear rule that pH and other measurement-based claim terms are interpreted under standard field conditions, providing predictability in ANDA litigation and formulation development.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies must draft formulation patent claims with precise measurement conditions or risk non-infringement findings where generic products differ under standardized measurement conditions.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor who cannot be located, and whether 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) allows a court to correct inventorship when the omitted inventor is unreachable.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents were invalid for failing to name a coinventor who could not be located, and upheld denial of inventorship correction under § 256(b). The decision underscores the risk companies face when collaborating with foreign manufacturers on product development without properly documenting and securing inventorship rights from all contributors.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can challenge patent validity based on omitted coinventors even where the patent holder acknowledges the error but cannot locate the missing inventor to effectuate correction.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign partners on product development face significant patent invalidity risk if foreign contributors' inventive contributions are not properly documented and inventorship is not correctly established from the outset.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the deadline for a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) in its original declaratory judgment action may obtain a mandatory stay by refiling a new declaratory judgment action and timely requesting the stay in the new case.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. This prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings and ensures that the statutory timeline for requesting a mandatory stay is strictly enforced.
impacts.positiveImplications: ITC complainants benefit from the assurance that respondents cannot manipulate parallel district court proceedings by strategically refiling declaratory judgment actions to obtain mandatory stays they previously failed to timely request.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies facing both ITC investigations and district court patent litigation must be vigilant about the 30-day deadline for requesting a mandatory stay, as missing the deadline cannot be cured by refiling the district court action.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where the Board failed to adequately address a claim limitation requiring reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay, and whether the court can review the Board's denial of a motion to terminate an IPR.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness finding invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, holding the Board failed to adequately address a specific claim limitation regarding time-delayed reporting. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. This decision highlights the importance of claim-by-claim analysis in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the requirement that the PTAB must specifically address each claim limitation in its obviousness analysis, providing meaningful appellate review of IPR final written decisions.
impacts.negativeImplications: IPR petitioners face the risk of vacatur and remand if the Board's obviousness analysis is insufficiently detailed regarding specific claim limitations, potentially prolonging expensive patent validity challenges.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million nationwide class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees, including approval of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary unlawfully used PACER fees to fund expenses beyond PACER operations. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting all objections raised by a pro se appellant.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement establishes that PACER fees must be limited to the cost of operating the PACER system, potentially reducing future fees for businesses and law firms that are heavy users of electronic court records.
